Heritage walk in Kolkata: Dalhousie, Chowringhee and the north

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

A heritage walk in Kolkata usually covers three areas: Dalhousie Square (BBD Bagh), the old administrative heart of the East India Company; Chowringhee and the Maidan, with the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial; and north Kolkata, where Bengali merchant families built rajbaris and the potters of Kumartuli still work. Each makes a comfortable two to three hour walk.

We arrange Kolkata heritage walks on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, led by an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, with other languages through partners.

Why Kolkata matters for Indian heritage

Kolkata (Calcutta) was the capital of British India from 1772 to 1911, and for most of that time the largest city the British governed in Asia. The administrative buildings, churches, cemeteries and clubs of that period survive in greater number here than almost anywhere else in the country. So does the other half of the story: the mansions, temples and printing presses of the Bengali families who traded with, worked for and argued against the Company.

That double history makes the city a strong classroom. On one street you can talk about the Company's revenue system, the Permanent Settlement, the Bengal renaissance and the swadeshi movement, using buildings rather than textbook diagrams. Our guide to Indian heritage explains how colonial buildings fit into the wider idea of what India protects and why.

Historical places in Kolkata: the layers by period

The city grew from three villages, Sutanuti, Gobindapur and Kalikata, where Job Charnock set up an English trading post in 1690. The first Fort William was built around 1700 near the river. After the Battle of Plassey (1757) the Company built a new, much larger Fort William on the Maidan and cleared the ground around it, which is why central Kolkata has such a wide open space.

Older communities left their mark too. Armenian merchants built the Church of Holy Nazareth in 1724, and Portuguese, Greek, Jewish and Chinese communities each had places of worship. Across the river and upstream, Bengali landholders and the Rani Rashmoni built temples such as Dakshineswar (1855).

PeriodWhat survives
Before 1757Armenian Church, St John's Church site, early cemeteries
1757 to 1850Raj Bhavan, South Park Street Cemetery, Shobhabazar Rajbari, Marble Palace
1850 to 1911GPO, Calcutta High Court, Indian Museum, Writers' Building facade
After 1911Victoria Memorial completed, Howrah Bridge, Nakhoda Masjid completed

Places a heritage walk in Kolkata covers

  1. Writers' Building 1777, facade remodelled 1880s

    Built for the Company's junior clerks (writers). Look at the red facade added later and the statues along the roof line.

  2. General Post Office 1864 to 1868

    Its domed hall stands on the site of the first Fort William. Brass markers in the area trace the old fort line.

  3. St John's Church 1787

    The first cathedral of Calcutta. Job Charnock's mausoleum in the grounds is among the oldest British structures in the city.

  4. Raj Bhavan 1799 to 1803

    Former Government House, modelled on Kedleston Hall in Derbyshire. Seen from outside; note the four wings and the gates.

  5. Calcutta High Court 1872

    Gothic Revival court building with a tall tower. A good place to discuss law, empire and Indian lawyers.

  6. Armenian Church of Holy Nazareth 1724

    One of the oldest churches in the city, with Armenian gravestones in the courtyard that predate the church.

  7. Indian Museum Founded 1814, building 1875

    India's oldest museum. Do not miss the Bharhut railing and gateway.

  8. St Paul's Cathedral 1847

    Indo-Gothic cathedral near the Maidan, rebuilt in part after earthquakes. Look at the stained glass.

  9. Victoria Memorial 1906 to 1921

    White Makrana marble memorial combining European and Mughal features, designed by William Emerson.

  10. South Park Street Cemetery 1767

    Tombs of 18th and early 19th century residents, including William Jones. Read the inscriptions slowly.

  11. Marble Palace 1835

    A merchant's mansion filled with European sculpture and paintings. Entry rules change, so check before you go.

  12. Jorasanko Thakur Bari 18th century

    The Tagore family home, where Rabindranath Tagore was born in 1861. Now part of Rabindra Bharati University.

  13. Shobhabazar Rajbari 18th century

    Built by Nabakrishna Deb, with a courtyard and thakur dalan used for Durga Puja. Shows how Bengali elites hosted festivals.

  14. Kumartuli Living tradition, 18th century onwards

    Lanes of image makers using river clay, straw and bamboo. Ask before photographing artisans at work.

  15. Dakshineswar Kali Temple 1855

    Navaratna temple built by Rani Rashmoni beside the Hooghly. Reached by vehicle or ferry.

Walking routes in Kolkata

Dalhousie Square on foot

About 2.5 hours

Writers' Building → General Post Office → St John's Church → Raj Bhavan → Calcutta High Court → Armenian Church of Holy Nazareth

Chowringhee and the Maidan

About 3 hours with the museum

Indian Museum → St Paul's Cathedral → Victoria Memorial → South Park Street Cemetery

North Kolkata houses and lanes

About 3 hours, short taxi hops between clusters

Jorasanko Thakur Bari → Marble Palace → Shobhabazar Rajbari → Kumartuli

Museums in Kolkata

  • Indian Museum. Bharhut sculpture, Gandhara galleries, coins and inscriptions. Allow at least two hours.
  • Victoria Memorial Hall. Paintings, maps and documents of colonial Calcutta, including works by Thomas and William Daniell.
  • Asutosh Museum of Indian Art. University of Calcutta collection strong on Bengal terracotta, textiles and folk art.
  • Rabindra Bharati Museum, Jorasanko. The Tagore house, with rooms on the family and the Bengal renaissance.

Best time for a walk

November to February, when mornings are cool and dry. Avoid the monsoon (June to September) and the week of Durga Puja unless the festival is the subject of the walk.

What you see on a heritage walk in Kolkata

In Dalhousie Square the walk reads the buildings as a system: the Writers' Building where Company clerks worked, the GPO raised on the site of the first Fort William, St John's Church with Job Charnock's mausoleum in its grounds, and the Calcutta High Court, modelled loosely on a Gothic cloth hall in Ypres. An archaeologist or historian will point out brick, stucco, cast iron imported from Britain and the way each building faces the square.

South Park Street Cemetery, opened in 1767, is one of the oldest surviving non-church cemeteries in the world. Its pyramids, obelisks and urns record soldiers, judges, children and scholars such as William Jones, founder of the Asiatic Society. Reading epitaphs is a good skill for older students; our lecture on cemeteries, epitaphs and public memory works well the week before.

North Kolkata is a different city. The Marble Palace (1835), Shobhabazar Rajbari and the Tagore family house at Jorasanko show how Bengali elites lived, collected and staged festivals. In Kumartuli the clay image makers work in narrow lanes, which opens a conversation about craft, caste, river clay and seasonal labour.

Museums in Kolkata

The Indian Museum, founded in 1814 by the Asiatic Society, is the oldest museum in India. Its galleries hold the Bharhut stupa railings and gateway (about the 2nd century BCE), Gandhara sculpture, coins and natural history. A morning here with someone who can read the sculpture changes how students see later temples; a museum gallery study with an archaeologist is the usual format.

The Victoria Memorial Hall has paintings, maps and documents of the colonial city, and the Asutosh Museum of Indian Art at the University of Calcutta is strong on Bengal terracotta and folk art.

Kolkata heritage walk for schools and colleges

For schools, the Dalhousie Square route is the easiest to manage: short distances, wide pavements on parts of the square and clear links to the CBSE and ICSE modern history syllabus. Keep groups to 25 to 30 students per guide so everyone can hear on busy streets. For colleges, north Kolkata and the cemetery suit students of history, sociology and architecture who can handle a slower, more interpretive walk.

We build Kolkata walks with each group, choosing the neighbourhoods and themes together. For a longer trip, our study tour of temples of eastern India or a study tour built for your group can add Bishnupur's terracotta temples or Santiniketan, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.

Practical advice for groups

Start early. Office traffic fills Dalhousie Square by 10 am on weekdays, so Sunday mornings are the calmest. Several buildings, including Raj Bhavan and the Writers' Building, are seen from outside only. Churches and the cemetery have their own visiting rules, and museums close one day a week, so check the ASI, museum or site website before you go.

Between north Kolkata and the centre, use the Metro or a hired bus rather than walking. For the full picture of the state, see our page on heritage sites in West Bengal.

Questions people ask

What are the best historical places in Kolkata for a first visit?

Start with Dalhousie Square (Writers' Building, GPO, St John's Church, High Court), then the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial. If you have a second morning, walk north Kolkata: Jorasanko, Marble Palace, Shobhabazar Rajbari and Kumartuli.

How long is a heritage walk in Kolkata?

Most routes take two to three hours on foot. A museum visit adds one to two hours. A full day can combine Dalhousie Square in the morning with the Indian Museum after lunch.

Is a Kolkata heritage walk suitable for school students?

Yes. The Dalhousie Square route has short distances and ties directly to modern Indian history in the CBSE and ICSE syllabus. Keep groups to about 25 to 30 students per guide and start early to avoid office traffic.

Which UNESCO World Heritage Sites are near Kolkata?

Santiniketan, inscribed in 2023, is about four hours away by road. The Sundarbans, a natural site, lies to the south. Neither is in the city itself, so plan them as separate day or overnight trips.

Can I see Raj Bhavan and the Writers' Building from inside?

Usually not. Both are working government buildings and are seen from outside on a walk. Rules can change, so check the official website before you plan a visit around them.
